why: Most product work is wasted on features nobody needed. Product Owners and Product Managers are hired to find the problems worth solving before the team builds anything, and to show the evidence behind each decision. Interviewers test this directly: “how do you know users want it?”
outcome: separate problems from solutions, plan and recruit for user research, run interviews that do not lead, turn notes into themes, personas and jobs to be done, build an opportunity solution tree, test risky assumptions with cheap prototypes, combine interviews with numbers and turn the research into clear decisions, including what not to build.

lessons.title: What discovery is and why most features fail
text: Product work has two halves. Discovery decides what is worth building; delivery builds it well. A team that skips discovery moves straight from an idea (“add a dashboard”) to a backlog item, and learns only after launch whether anyone needed it. Many shipped features end up rarely used or fail to move the metric they were meant to move. The code is usually fine: the problem was misunderstood, too rare to matter, or not painful enough for anyone to change their habits.

The core habit is to separate the problem space from the solution space. The problem space is about people: who they are, what they are trying to get done, what gets in their way, how they cope today and what that costs them. The solution space is about the product: screens, features, integrations, pricing. Customers and stakeholders almost always arrive with solutions (“we need an export to Excel”). The Product Owner’s job is to go back to the problem (“what do you do with the export?”) before choosing between several possible solutions.

The Double Diamond, published by the UK Design Council, draws the same idea: first diverge to explore the problem widely, then converge on one problem definition; then diverge again to explore several solutions, and converge on the one to deliver. Teams that jump to the second diamond skip the work that makes the solution relevant.

Modern teams do not treat discovery as a phase before the project. In dual-track agile (a term from Desirée Sy, made popular by Jeff Patton and Marty Cagan), discovery and delivery run in parallel in the same team. Each week the product trio (product manager or owner, designer, tech lead) talks to a few users and tests ideas, while developers build items that already passed discovery. Teresa Torres calls this continuous discovery: weekly contact with customers by the team that builds the product.

In interviews for Product Owner and Product Manager roles, expect “How do you know a problem is worth solving?” and “Tell me about an idea you stopped after discovery.” Hiring managers listen for habits: how often you talk to users, what evidence you collect, and one concrete case where a finding changed a decision.
points: Discovery lowers the risk of building the wrong thing; delivery builds what passed.
Start in the problem space: who, what they try to do, what blocks them, what it costs.
Stakeholder requests are solutions: ask what problem they solve before accepting them.
Dual-track: discovery and delivery run every week, in the same team (the product trio).
Continuous discovery beats one big study a year: a few conversations every week.

example.code:
Stakeholder request: "Add an export to Excel on the orders page."

Problem-space questions:
  - Who exports, and how often?
  - What do they do with the file next?
  - What happens when they cannot do it?

Finding (5 interviews): 4 of 5 export to build a weekly late-orders list for their manager.
Real problem: "I cannot see which orders are late without rebuilding the list by hand."

Solution options:
  A. Late-orders filter on the orders page
  B. Weekly e-mail summary of late orders
  C. Excel export (still possible, now one option among three)
example.note: The request was a solution. Going back to the problem opened two cheaper options that serve the real need better.

lessons.title: Planning research: goals, participants, recruiting and consent
text: Good research starts from a decision, not from curiosity. Write down what the team must decide (“do we build a late-orders view this quarter?”) and what you need to learn to decide it. Then separate research questions, which are what you want to learn (“how do shop owners track late orders today?”), from interview questions, which are what you actually ask a participant (“tell me about the last time an order was late”). Mixing them up produces interviews that ask users to do your analysis for you.

Choose the method that fits the question. Generative research explores problems you do not understand yet: exploratory interviews, field visits and contextual inquiry (watching people do the work where they do it). Evaluative research checks a solution: usability tests of a prototype, A/B tests, beta programmes. Early in a topic, generative interviews come first; once you have a candidate solution, evaluative tests take over.

Decide who to talk to before recruiting. Pick the segment that matters for the decision, and prefer people who did the behaviour recently: they remember facts, not opinions. Include people who are not happy customers: churned users, prospects who chose a competitor, users of a spreadsheet workaround. Write a short screener (three to five questions) to check that each participant fits. For exploratory interviews, teams often plan five to eight per segment and stop when they stop hearing anything new (saturation); for usability tests, Jakob Nielsen’s well-known advice is small rounds of about five users, repeated after each fix.

Recruiting is where plans fail in real jobs. Sources: an in-app invitation, customer success and sales contacts, a newsletter, a research panel. Watch for bias: the customers sales hands you are often the happiest ones, and power users are not typical. Offer a modest thank-you (a voucher) that does not depend on what people say, recruit one or two more than you need because some will not show up, and book 30 to 45 minutes.

Ethics and consent are part of the plan. Tell participants the purpose, what is recorded, who will see it, how long it is kept and that they can stop at any time, and get their agreement before recording. In the European Union, interview notes and recordings are personal data under the GDPR: collect only what you need, store recordings in an access-controlled place, pseudonymise notes (P1, P2…) and delete raw recordings when the retention period ends. Never sell during a research session, and take extra care with minors or vulnerable people.
points: Start from the decision the research must inform.
Research questions (what you want to learn) are not interview questions (what you ask).
Generative research explores problems; evaluative research checks solutions.
Recruit people who did the behaviour recently, with a screener; plan for no-shows.
Informed consent before recording; under the GDPR, minimise, protect and delete.

example.code:
RESEARCH PLAN (one page)
Decision:  Build a late-orders view in Q3, or not?
Learn:     How do shop owners spot and handle late orders today? How often? What does it cost them?
Method:    6 exploratory interviews (video, 40 min) + review 3 months of support tickets tagged "delivery"
Who:       Shop owners with 50+ orders a week, at least one late order in the last 2 weeks
Screener:  orders per week? last late order? who handles it? tools used?
Recruit:   in-app invitation + customer success list (max 2 from CS), 8 invited for 6 slots
Thank-you: 30 EUR voucher, same for everyone
Consent:   purpose, recording, access (product trio only), recordings deleted after 6 months
Team:      PO interviews, designer takes notes, tech lead joins 2 sessions
Readout:   Friday week 3, 30 min, with the decision on the agenda
example.note: One page is enough. The decision line keeps the study short and useful.

lessons.title: User interviews that do not lead
text: A leading question puts the answer in the question: “Wouldn’t it be useful to get an alert when an order is late?” People are polite, they want to help, and they say yes. Questions about the future are just as weak: “Would you use…?”, “How much would you pay for…?” produce optimistic guesses, not facts. The interview then confirms what the team already believed, and the feature fails after launch.

Rob Fitzpatrick’s book The Mom Test (2013) gives three rules that fit on a card: talk about their life instead of your idea; ask about specifics in the past instead of generalities or opinions about the future; talk less and listen more. The name comes from the idea that even your mother cannot mislead you with kind words if you ask about what she actually did, not about what she thinks of your idea.

So ask for stories about real past events. “Tell me about the last time an order was late.” “What happened next?” “How did you find out?” “What did you do about it?” “What did that cost you, in time or money?” “What have you already tried?” Specific stories reveal the real workflow, the workarounds and the size of the pain. When someone says “I usually…” or “I always…”, bring them back to one instance: “Can you walk me through the last time?”

A good interview has a simple flow: introduction and consent, a short warm-up about their role and context, the story of a recent event, digging deeper (why, what else, who else), their current solutions and workarounds, then a wrap-up (“Is there anything I should have asked?”, “Who else should I talk to?”) and thanks. Let silences run, follow up with “tell me more”, and do not pitch. If you show a prototype, do it at the end: that part is an evaluative test, not discovery.

Listen for the difference between noise and signal. Compliments (“great idea!”), generic claims and feature ideas are not evidence. Signals are facts about past behaviour, workarounds people built (spreadsheets, scripts, manual checks), money or time already spent, and commitments: accepting a pilot, introducing you to their manager, pre-ordering. One person asks the questions and a second takes notes, so the interviewer can listen.
points: No leading questions: never put the answer in the question.
Ask about specific past events, not opinions about the future.
“Tell me about the last time…” is the strongest opening.
Workarounds, time or money spent and commitments are signals; compliments are not.
Do not pitch during discovery; show prototypes only at the end, as a test.

example.code:
LEADING / WEAK                                   OPEN / PAST BEHAVIOUR
"Would you use a late-orders alert?"             "Tell me about the last time an order was late."
"Don't you find tracking orders painful?"        "How do you find out that an order is late?"
"How much would you pay for this?"               "What have you spent on this problem so far?"
"Do you like our new dashboard?"                 "Walk me through what you did on Monday morning."
"Is speed important to you?"                     "What did you do the last time it was slow?"
example.note: Each question on the right asks for a fact the participant remembers; each on the left asks for an opinion or suggests the answer.

lessons.title: Synthesis: affinity mapping, personas and jobs to be done
text: Raw notes are not insights. Synthesis starts right after each interview with a short debrief (10 to 15 minutes) while memories are fresh. Teresa Torres suggests an interview snapshot: one page per interview with a memorable quote, quick facts about the participant, the opportunities (needs and pain points) heard and the insights. Separate what the person said or did (observation) from what you think it means (interpretation).

Affinity mapping (also called the KJ method, after Jiro Kawakita) groups observations from the bottom up. Write one observation per note, put all the notes from all interviews on a wall or a digital board, and move similar notes together without deciding the categories in advance. Then name each group with a sentence that says what it means (“Late orders are found by customers, not by the shop”). Count how many participants mention each theme, not how many notes: one talkative person can fill a wall.

A persona is a short, research-based description of a type of user: their goals, context, behaviours and pain points, with a name to make it easy to talk about. Useful personas are few (two to four) and built from patterns seen in several interviews. Invented demographic details (age, hobbies) add nothing. A proto-persona written from assumptions before research is fine as a starting point, as long as everyone knows it still has to be checked.

Jobs to be done (JTBD), made popular by Clayton Christensen, looks at the progress people try to make in a given situation: they “hire” a product to get a job done. A job story writes it as: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]. Seen this way, your competitors are whatever people hire today, including a spreadsheet, a phone call or doing nothing. Bob Moesta’s forces of progress explain switching: the push of the current problem and the pull of the new solution must beat the anxiety about the new solution and the habit of the present one.

In interviews, explain synthesis as a process, not a feeling: “we tag every observation, group them, count participants per theme and check the strongest themes against support tickets.” Hiring managers want to hear that you report how much evidence sits behind each insight.
points: Debrief within the hour; keep observations apart from interpretations.
Affinity mapping groups notes bottom-up; name each group with a meaningful sentence.
Count participants per theme, not notes.
Personas come from patterns in research; few, short, without invented details.
Job story: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome].

example.code:
AFFINITY MAP (6 interviews, P1-P6)
Theme                                              Participants
Late orders are found by customers, not the shop   P1 P2 P4 P5 P6   (5/6)
The late list is rebuilt by hand every week        P2 P3 P5         (3/6)
Carriers' tracking pages are checked one by one    P1 P4            (2/6)

JOB STORY
When a customer writes to ask where their order is,
I want to see at once which orders are late and why,
so I can answer before they ask for a refund.

TODAY'S "COMPETITORS": a weekly spreadsheet, carriers' websites, apologising to customers
example.note: Themes are sentences with a participant count; the job story keeps the situation and the outcome, not a feature.

lessons.title: Opportunity solution trees: choosing what to explore
text: The opportunity solution tree is a visual tool from Teresa Torres, described in her book Continuous Discovery Habits (2021). At the top sits the desired outcome: a measurable change the team can influence. Under it are opportunities: customer needs, pain points and desires found in research, written from the customer’s point of view. Under each opportunity sit several possible solutions, and under each solution the assumption tests that will show whether it works.

The top of the tree must be an outcome, not an output. An output is something the team ships (“a late-orders dashboard”); an outcome is a change in behaviour or results (“reduce ‘where is my order?’ tickets from 400 to 250 a month”). Torres distinguishes business outcomes (revenue, retention) from product outcomes, which the team can move directly and which drive the business outcome. A good product outcome is specific, measurable and within the team’s influence.

Opportunities are not features in disguise. “Shop owners need a dashboard” is a solution; “I do not know an order is late until the customer complains” is an opportunity. Large opportunities break down into smaller ones until each is small enough to work on. To choose a target opportunity, compare sibling opportunities rather than judging each alone: how many customers it affects and how often (opportunity sizing), how important it is to them, how well it fits the company’s strategy and whether competitors already solve it well.

Once the target opportunity is chosen, generate several solutions, ideally at least three, before falling in love with one. Torres warns against “whether or not” decisions (“should we build X?”): comparing options gives better answers. Each solution then gets its riskiest assumptions tested quickly, and the tree stays visible and up to date as the team learns.

The tree is also a communication tool. When a stakeholder asks “why aren’t we building my feature?”, the tree shows the outcome, the opportunity it serves (or does not), and the alternatives being tested. Credit the method to Teresa Torres when you mention it in an interview: hiring managers often know her work.
points: Desired outcome at the top, then opportunities, solutions and assumption tests.
Outcome = measurable change in behaviour or results; output = what we ship.
Opportunities are needs or pain points in the customer’s words, not features.
Choose a target opportunity by comparing siblings: size, importance, strategy, market.
Compare at least three solutions; avoid “whether or not” decisions.

example.code:
OUTCOME: "Where is my order?" tickets from 400 to 250 a month
|
+-- Opportunity: "I only learn an order is late when the customer complains"   <- target
|   +-- Solution A: late-orders filter on the orders page
|   |     Test: 5 owners find today's late orders on a clickable prototype
|   +-- Solution B: daily e-mail listing late orders
|   |     Test: concierge, send the list by hand to 10 shops for 2 weeks
|   +-- Solution C: automatic delay message to the customer
|         Test: fake door "Notify customers automatically" in settings
|
+-- Opportunity: "I cannot tell customers a reliable delivery date"
+-- Opportunity: "Carriers' tracking pages are slow to check one by one"
example.note: Three solutions for one target opportunity, each with its own small test. The other opportunities stay on the tree for later.

lessons.title: Assumptions and how to test them
text: Every solution rests on assumptions that must be true for it to work. Marty Cagan (Inspired) names four product risks: value (will customers buy or choose to use it? often called desirability), usability (can they figure out how to use it?), feasibility (can we build it with our time, skills and technology?) and business viability (does it work for the business: costs, legal, sales, support?). List the assumptions of each solution under these four headings, written as statements: “Shop owners check the late-orders list at least once a day.”

You cannot test everything, so prioritise. Assumption mapping, popularised by David Bland, places each assumption on two axes: how important it is to the idea’s success, and how much evidence you already have. Test first the assumptions that are important and have little evidence, often called leap-of-faith assumptions. The well-known, low-impact ones can wait.

Pick the cheapest test that gives real evidence. Desirability: a fake door (also called a painted door: a button or menu entry for a feature that does not exist yet, which measures clicks), a landing page smoke test, pre-orders or a waitlist. Concierge test: deliver the service by hand to a few customers, openly, to learn what they really value. Wizard of Oz: the customer sees what looks like an automated product, but people do the work behind the scenes. Usability: a clickable prototype tested with about five users on realistic tasks while they think aloud. Feasibility: a technical spike or proof of concept by engineers. Viability: check with finance, legal, sales and support, and work out the unit costs.

Write the success criterion before running the test: “At least 5 % of owners who see the button click it within two weeks” or “4 of 5 users complete the task without help.” Without a threshold decided in advance, any result can be read as a success. Keep tests small and fast: days, not months.

Fake doors need care. Tell users honestly what happened after the click (“Coming soon: join the waitlist”), never take payment for something you will not deliver, and do not leave a fake door in place for months. In interviews, a good answer names the risk, the test, the threshold and what the team did with the result.
points: Four risks: value (desirability), usability, feasibility, business viability.
Test first what is important and has little evidence (leap of faith).
Fake door, smoke test, concierge, Wizard of Oz, prototype test, technical spike: choose the cheapest that answers.
Write the success criterion before the test starts.
Be honest with users after a fake door; never charge for what does not exist.

example.code:
ASSUMPTION TEST CARD
Assumption:  Shop owners want late orders flagged automatically     (risk: value)
Evidence so far: 5 of 6 interviews; no behaviour data
Test:        Fake door: "Flag late orders" switch in Settings, then "Coming soon - join the waitlist"
Audience:    all shops with 50+ orders a week, 2 weeks
Success if:  at least 5 % of owners who open Settings click the switch
Result:      2,500 saw it, 170 clicked (6.8 %), 63 joined the waitlist
Decision:    passes; next, prototype test of the late-orders filter (risk: usability)
example.note: Risk, test, threshold and decision on one card. The threshold was written before the data came in.

lessons.title: Quantitative signals that complement interviews
text: Interviews explain why; numbers show how many and how often. Neither is enough alone. A common loop: analytics shows where users drop (for example, 40 % abandon the shipping step), interviews explain why, then the numbers size the problem and later show whether the fix worked. When interviews, analytics and support tickets point the same way, you have triangulation, and much more confidence.

Product analytics answers behaviour questions: funnels (where people leave a flow), retention cohorts (do users who started in March come back?), feature adoption (share of active users who used a feature) and segmentation (mobile vs desktop, small vs large customers). The numbers are only as good as the tracking plan: check that events are defined, named consistently and firing before you trust a chart.

Surveys measure how widespread something is, not why. Use closed questions for sizing, one idea per question (no double-barrelled questions such as “Is the app fast and easy?”), neutral wording and answer options that cover every case. Watch who answers: people who reply to a survey are rarely a random sample. The margin of error at 95 % confidence for a share p from n answers is about 1.96 × √(p × (1 − p) / n): with 400 answers and 30 %, that is about ±4.5 points. Sean Ellis’ question “How would you feel if you could no longer use the product?” (very disappointed / somewhat / not) is often used as a signal of product/market fit, with 40 % “very disappointed” as his suggested benchmark.

Support tickets, sales call notes, app store reviews and open comments in NPS surveys are free research. Tag them by theme, count them per month and follow the trend: a theme that grows is an opportunity. Search logs (what users type in your search box) show what they expect to find. These sources come from people who were motivated to write, so use them to spot and size themes, then interview to understand them.

A frequent mistake in real jobs is to ask a survey to do discovery (“Would you use feature X?”). The answers are opinions about the future, the same weakness as leading interview questions. Use surveys to measure something you already understand from interviews.
points: Interviews tell why; analytics and surveys tell how many and how often.
Triangulate: interviews + analytics + support tickets pointing the same way.
Trust analytics only after checking the tracking plan.
Surveys: one idea per question, neutral wording, watch who answers, state the margin of error.
Support tickets and reviews: tag, count, follow the trend.

example.code:
A1  Answer                 B1  Respondents   C1  Share
A2  Very disappointed      B2  120           C2  =B2/$B$5
A3  Somewhat disappointed  B3  170           C3  =B3/$B$5
A4  Not disappointed       B4  110           C4  =B4/$B$5
A5  Total                  B5  =SUM(B2:B4)
D2  =1.96*SQRT(C2*(1-C2)/$B$5)
example.note: 120 / 400 = 30 % very disappointed, below Sean Ellis’ 40 % benchmark. D2 gives the margin of error: about 0.045, so 30 % ± 4.5 points.

lessons.title: From research to decisions
text: Research only matters if it changes what the team does. Share insights, not transcripts: an insight is an observation, why it matters and the evidence behind it (how many participants, a quote, a number). A 30-minute readout with the decision on the agenda, a two-minute clip of real users, and an insight repository where notes are tagged and searchable reach far more people than a 40-page report. Inviting stakeholders and developers to watch interviews is the fastest way to build shared understanding.

Turn the research into a problem statement the team can rally around. A useful template: [User] needs a way to [need] because [insight]. Today they [workaround], which costs [impact]. We will know we have solved it when [outcome metric]. Teams also reframe it as “How might we…?” questions to open the solution space, for example “How might we let owners spot late orders before their customers do?”

Discovery ends in a decision for each idea: build (the risky assumptions passed), iterate (promising but a test failed, change and retest), pivot (the problem is real but the solution is wrong) or stop. Write each decision in a decision log with the date, the evidence and what would make you reconsider. Saying what you will not build is a real output of discovery: every idea you drop frees the team for something better.

Saying no to a stakeholder works best with evidence and an alternative: “We tested the export idea: 4 of 5 owners wanted to find late orders, not a file. We are building the late-orders filter first and will check in six weeks whether exports are still requested.” Tie the answer to the shared outcome, not to opinions.

When an idea passes discovery, hand it to delivery with context: the problem statement, the evidence, the success metric, the prototype and open questions. The backlog items and acceptance criteria come from there, and the success metric is checked after release, which starts the next discovery cycle.
points: Insight = observation + why it matters + evidence.
Short readouts, clips and an insight repository beat long reports.
Problem statement: who, need, insight, today’s workaround, impact, success metric.
Each idea ends as build, iterate, pivot or stop, written in a decision log.
Deciding what not to build is a result of discovery, not a failure.

example.code:
PROBLEM STATEMENT
Shop owners with 50+ orders a week need a way to spot late orders early,
because 5 of 6 learn about a delay only when the customer complains.
Today they rebuild a late-orders list by hand every week (about 1 hour),
which costs time and refunds.
We will know we solved it when "where is my order?" tickets fall from 400 to 250 a month.

DECISION LOG
Date        Idea                     Evidence                                Decision   Revisit if
2026-03-04  Late-orders filter       6.8 % fake-door clicks; 5/5 found it    Build      -
2026-03-04  Excel export             1/5 needed the file itself              Stop       export requests > 20/month
2026-03-04  Auto message to customer Legal: consent wording unclear          Iterate    legal review done
example.note: The statement keeps the user, the evidence and the metric together; the log records why each idea was built, changed or stopped.

pitfalls: Treating a stakeholder’s feature request as the problem instead of asking what it is for.
Asking leading or future questions (“Would you use…?”) and counting the polite yes as validation.
Interviewing only friendly power users or the customers sales picks.
Counting notes instead of participants, so one talkative person becomes a “trend”.
Putting an output (“launch the dashboard”) at the top of the opportunity solution tree.
Running a test without a success criterion written beforehand, then reading any result as a win.
Ending discovery without a written decision, so the team builds everything anyway.

exercises.q: Sort these interview questions: leading or weak, or open and about past behaviour.

groups.name: Leading or weak
items: Would you use an alert for late orders?
Don’t you find tracking deliveries painful?
How much would you pay for this feature?
Do you like our new design?

groups.name: Open, past behaviour
items: Tell me about the last time an order was late.
How did you find out about it?
What have you already tried to fix this?
What happened next?

exercises.answer: Leading questions put the answer in the question; future and price questions produce optimistic guesses; “do you like” asks for a compliment. Questions about a specific past event bring facts: what happened, how they coped, what it cost.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a discovery interview in order.
steps: Introduce yourself, explain the purpose and get consent to record
Warm up: their role and context
Ask for the story of a recent, specific event
Dig deeper: why, what else, who else was involved
Explore their current workarounds and what they cost
Wrap up: anything I should have asked? Who else should I talk to?
exercises.answer: Consent first, then context, then a concrete story, digging, current solutions and a wrap-up that often brings new leads. No pitch anywhere in the flow.

exercises.q: Match each risk with a test that addresses it well.
pairs: Five users try a clickable prototype while thinking aloud
Engineers build a short technical spike
Review costs, legal terms and support load with finance and legal
exercises.answer: Each of Marty Cagan’s four risks needs a different kind of evidence: behaviour for value, observed use for usability, engineering work for feasibility, and business partners for viability.

exercises.q: The Head of Sales says: “Our biggest prospect needs a custom reporting module. Put it in the next sprint.”

choices.label: Ask what the prospect wants to achieve with the reports and offer to join a call with them
choices.feedback: You go back to the problem space and get first-hand evidence, without saying no yet.

choices.label: Add it to the next sprint: the deal is big
choices.feedback: You commit the team to a solution nobody has examined; one prospect’s request may not fit other customers.

choices.label: Refuse: the roadmap is fixed
choices.feedback: A flat no damages the relationship and ignores a possible real opportunity.

steps.text: The call shows they need a weekly view of late deliveries for their managers. Two other customers said the same in interviews. Next?

choices.label: Add the opportunity to the tree, compare solutions (filter, e-mail summary, report) and test the most promising one quickly
choices.feedback: The need is confirmed by several customers; comparing options often finds something cheaper than a custom module.

choices.label: Build the custom module exactly as sales described it
choices.feedback: You would skip the comparison and build the most expensive option for one customer.

steps.text: How do you reply to the Head of Sales?

choices.label: Share the evidence, the option you are testing, its date and how the prospect can take part in the test
choices.feedback: Evidence, a plan and a role for the prospect turn a demand into a shared decision.

choices.label: Say nothing until the feature is ready
choices.feedback: Silence makes sales escalate; stakeholders need to see the reasoning and the timing.

exercises.answer: Treat the request as a signal: find the problem behind it, check whether other customers share it, compare several solutions against the team’s outcome, test the best one and keep the stakeholder involved with evidence and dates.

exercises.q: Which is the best desired outcome for the top of an opportunity solution tree?
options: Launch the late-orders dashboard in Q3
Reduce “where is my order?” tickets from 400 to 250 a month
exercises.answer: An outcome is a measurable change the team can influence. Launching a dashboard is an output, “happier” is not measurable as written, and interviews are an activity.

exercises.q: After an interview, which one is the strongest signal that the problem is real and worth solving?
options: The participant said “That’s a great idea, I would definitely use it”
The participant built a spreadsheet they update by hand every week to work around the problem
The participant suggested five new features
The participant rated the problem 8 out of 10
exercises.answer: Time already spent on a workaround is past behaviour: it proves the pain and its cost. Compliments, feature ideas and ratings are opinions.

exercises.q: In an opportunity solution tree, the top node is the desired ___ (one word).
exercises.answer: Outcome: a measurable change in behaviour or results that the team can influence, such as fewer support tickets or higher weekly use. Opportunities, solutions and assumption tests sit under it.

exercises.q: Excel on a real sheet: Sean Ellis survey. In C2, the share of respondents who would be very disappointed without the product.
exercises.hint: Divide the “very disappointed” count by the total of all answers.
exercises.explain: =B2/SUM(B2:B4) gives 84 / 280 = 0.30, so 30 % very disappointed, below the 40 % benchmark Sean Ellis suggests for product/market fit. Using SUM instead of typing 280 keeps the formula right when answers are added.

exercises.q: Excel on a real sheet: eight interviews. In F2, the average minutes lost per week among the participants who mentioned late orders.
exercises.hint: AVERAGEIFS starts with the range to average, then a range and its condition.
exercises.explain: =AVERAGEIFS(D2:D9,C2:C9,"Yes") averages 45, 90, 30, 120, 60 and 75: 420 / 6 = 70 minutes a week. Six of eight participants mentioned the problem, and those who did lose more than an hour a week: a useful size for the problem statement.

exercises.q: Excel on a real sheet: a fake door ran for two weeks. In F2, the click rate over both weeks (clicks divided by visitors who saw the button).
exercises.hint: Add the clicks, add the visitors, then divide. Do not average the two weekly rates.
exercises.explain: =SUM(C2:C3)/SUM(B2:B3) gives 170 / 2,500 = 0.068, a 6.8 % click rate, above a 5 % success criterion set in advance. Averaging the weekly rates (6.5 % and 7.08 %) would weight both weeks equally although they had different traffic.

exercises.q: Written: an online grocery app sees many customers abandon their basket at the delivery slot step. Write six interview questions for a discovery interview on this problem (no leading questions, no questions about the future).
exercises.answer: Model answer (any open questions about specific past events work): 1) Tell me about the last time you did your grocery shopping online: what were you doing that day? 2) Walk me through how you chose a delivery slot that time. 3) What happened when the slot you wanted was not available? 4) What did you do next: wait, change the slot, use another shop? 5) How do you usually plan when your groceries arrive? Can you tell me about the last week you had to change a delivery? 6) What have you tried before to get groceries at a time that suits you, and what did it cost you? Avoid: “Would you pay for a faster slot?”, “Don’t you find the slots confusing?”, “Would you like more slots?”

interview.q: How do you know a problem is worth solving?
interview.a: I look for evidence on three fronts. Frequency and reach: how many users hit it and how often, from analytics and support tickets. Pain: what it costs them today, shown by workarounds, time or money spent. Fit: whether it moves the outcome our team owns and fits the strategy. If interviews, numbers and tickets point the same way, I am confident; if only one source says so, I run a small test before committing the team.

interview.q: How do you run a user interview?
interview.a: I start from the decision the research supports and recruit people who did the behaviour recently, with a screener and consent to record. In the session I ask about specific past events (“tell me about the last time…”), dig with follow-ups, explore workarounds and never pitch. A colleague takes notes, we debrief right after, and I write a snapshot of each interview so the synthesis is fast.

interview.q: What is the difference between an outcome and an output?
interview.a: An output is what we ship, such as a dashboard; an outcome is the change it should create, such as support tickets falling from 400 to 250 a month or more users completing a task. I set goals as outcomes so the team can choose the best solution and so we can tell whether a release worked.

interview.q: A stakeholder insists on a specific feature. What do you do?
interview.a: I treat it as a signal, not an order. I ask what problem it solves and for whom, ideally join a call with the customer behind it, and check whether others share the need. Then I compare several solutions against our outcome and test the most promising one. I come back with evidence, a decision and dates, and if we do not build it, I explain why and what would change my mind.

interview.q: Tell me about an assumption you tested. How did you test it?
interview.a: A good answer names the assumption, its risk type, the test and the threshold. For example: we assumed shop owners wanted late orders flagged automatically (value risk). We added a fake door in Settings for two weeks with a success criterion of 5 % clicks; 6.8 % clicked and 63 joined the waitlist, so we moved to a prototype test for usability before building.

interview.q: What is an opportunity solution tree and why use it?
interview.a: It is Teresa Torres’ visual map from Continuous Discovery Habits: a desired outcome at the top, opportunities from research under it, several solutions per opportunity and assumption tests under each solution. It keeps the team focused on the outcome, forces us to compare options instead of debating one idea, and shows stakeholders why we work on what we work on.

interview.q: How do you combine qualitative and quantitative research?
interview.a: Numbers show where and how much, interviews show why. I usually find a drop or a theme in analytics or tickets, interview users to understand it, then size it with data or a short survey, and measure the effect after release. When the sources agree, I act with confidence; when they disagree, that is a finding to investigate.

interview.q: How do you share research so it changes decisions?
interview.a: Short and decision-focused: a 30-minute readout with the decision on the agenda, insights with their evidence (how many participants, a quote, a number), a few short clips, and a searchable repository. I invite stakeholders and developers to watch interviews, and I record each decision, including what we chose not to build, in a decision log.
